metadata.title: [Fix]: Filter system should work in world space and then restore projection transform.

issue_payload.body: See https://github.com/pixijs/pixi.js/pull/7044#issuecomment-739322922 Basically, instead of making the filtering pipeline work in projected space (if `projectionSystem.transform` is applied) - we should make it work in world space. This would simplify all our calculations b/c we don't have to worry about the projection transform. The projection transform is restored when rendering to the final output texture in `bindAndClear`. Another benefit is that applying filtering in projected space can increase the AABB (think rotation), which is unwanted. ## Other changes I and @ivanpopelyshev had a call and we coded together and did the following fixes: * restore the sourceFrame/destinationFrame binding of the render texture system * apply the rounding of the filter system's source frame in screen space (by projecting it there, rounding, and projecting it back). We skip rounding if the projection has skew involved, since that invalidates the "rectangleness". * added the fix in #6892, #6893 (the "fix regression in y-flipping PR") since it wasn't already in the `main` branch but in `development`. (It was creating a problem in our testing so we had to "pre-merge" it) - [ ] Tests and/or benchmarks are included - [ ] Documentation is changed or added - [ ] Lint process passed (`npm run lint`) - [ ] Tests passed (`npm run test`)

@dev7355608 

I understand your reasoning for 2 now. But I still feel `filterArea` should be transformed because the two cases you show do have a fundamental difference. Think about it like this:

First case: You are moving a sheet of paper (i.e. transforming the world).

Second case: You are moving the contents of the paper (i.e. transforming the stage).

Since the `filterArea` is defined in the sheet of paper, it must be transformed in the first case; but not in the second.

For 3, your analogy doesn't make sense, because `FilterSystem.push` doesn't assign a _new_ projection matrix. It would look more like this:

```
push()                    projection.transform === matrix1
    child1_render()  projection.transform === null (rendering from world directly into render-texture, without extra projection)
    
    child2_push()    projection.transform === null (as before)
    child2_render()
    child2_pop()     projection.transform ===  Matrix.IDENTITY (nothing to restore)

    child3_render()  projection.transform === Matrix.IDENTITY
pop()                    projection.transform will be set to matrix1 (restored in bindAndClear())
```

If there is a chance that `bindAndClear` is never called on the output render-texture, we should also restore the `projection.transform` in the end of `pop()`. I think that's what you mean (not set it to `null`).

discussion_timeline.body:
The reason we switched was because of the textBaseline property when rendering text on canvas. Originally this was set to 'top'. Different browsers render 'top' in different locations. Therefore the text was being placed in different spots on different browsers. Using 'alphabetic' (the default setting for textBaseline), however, puts the font in the same place on every browser. But in order to accurately position the baseline in the same place, you have to know the ascent of the rendered  font, not the height. And you can't consistently guess the ascent based off of the height (like multiplying by 0.75 to guess) because some fonts have unusually high ascents (like Oswald).

Also, the method that was used before basically injected text into the dom and measured the height but that returned different values for different browsers. What this meant was that if you had multiple lines of text going down the page in one text element (like 10 lines for example) then the tenth line would be in a completely different place depending on the browser (line height \* 10).

This also seems a bit nitpicky for the use case of making a game where close enough is close enough and usually you won't have 10 lines of text running down the page. In that case you can just adjust things so close enough is close enough. 

However, I've written an editor for creating animatable websites in PIXI.JS.

Examples are here to give you an idea of what I'm talking about: 

example-designer.makemake.io
example-photography.makemake.io
example-planets.makemake.io

The editor is at makemake.io if you need to look at that to understand what I'm talking about.

Anyway, in the editor the user is picking a google web font on the fly and then putting as many lines of text in as they need. So the manual adjustment strategy doesn't really work. It needs to be accurate across different browsers and devices. Anyway, pixel scanning pretty much works but every once in a while I have bizarre issues on mobile devices where its wildly off and text gets clipped and I can't tell if this is due to my implementation or what.

Hopefully I will get ahold of a mobile device where the problem happens consistently and I can hook up a remote debugger to it.

Also, some commentary on the current implementation in the dev branch - according to the spec, actualboundingboxascent returns the ascent of the measured line of text. So first we're trying pixel scanning an |Mq and say we get value of 10 for the ascent. And then we get the actualboundingboxascent (in a browser that supports it) of _each line of text_ which happens to be let's say  "_____" then that will return 1 or 2. Actualboundingboxascent overrides the pixel scanned font ascent if the actualboundboxascent is found. That seems like a problem. We should be getting the ascent of the font, not each line of text. Please note that I haven't tested this, but the code just looks wacky because it's measuring different text samples to compute the same property.

Ok, this post has gotten really long and I haven't suggested a solution. In any case, as I said before I'll try to figure it out as best I can when I get a chance.

BTW, whatever solution we come up with will probably never be exactly exactly the same all the time for webfonts since different browsers are consuming different file formats of the same font.

Thanks,
Eric

discussion_timeline.body:
I can see both sides of the coin.

Generally when we are removing something from a container, it is because we are cleaning up and destroying resources (e.g. when a page switch occurs, or when a sprite/particle is no longer needed). Comparing with other libs, such as `jQueryObj.remove( child )`, [EaselJS](http://createjs.com/Docs/EaselJS/classes/Container.html#method_removeChild), and many others, most devs won't expect this to throw an error when the child has already been removed.

discussion_timeline.body:
@ivanpopelyshev I pushed changes to make the tests to pass. I following breaking changes will occur:

* Display objects that have a change in their natural bounds will _have to declare that by updating `_boundsID`_. They will not get bounds update for free as before (because `updateTransform` will not be called if bounds are already update-to-date in `getLocalBounds`).

---

discussion_timeline.author: bigtimebuddy

discussion_timeline.author: ShukantPal
discussion_timeline.body:
@bigtimebuddy I'll explain the "breaking" change a bit rigorously as follows:

Let's say we have a display-object `object`;  it is (and was) expected that if its transform has not changed and `object._boundsID` is not dirty then`object.getBounds()` will calculate the same bounds.

Now, the local bounds are, by definition, defined as bounds _without any transforms applied_. That leaves us with: if `object._boundsID` is not marked dirty, then `object.getLocalBounds()` will calculate the same value.

---

Previously, `getLocalBounds` always deferred to `getBounds` - which always did an `updateTransform`. Now, `updateTransform` marks `_boundsID` dirty, well because it thinks that the transform has changed.

Hence, since `_boundsID` was made dirty internally in `getLocalBounds` - that meant `calculateBounds` was called each and every time `getLocalBounds` was called, and that authors of display-objects (like `PIXI.Graphics#clear()`) did not have to worry about marking their bounds dirty.

**This assumption is now incorrect with this PR**. If `object._boundsID` is in-sync with `this._bounds.updateID`, then the local bounds won't be updated.

---

## Why?

By _not_ updating the local bounds when they aren't marked dirty, we prevent unnecessary bounds calculations and transform updates.

## Future work

Similarly, we could prevent `getBounds()` updates if the transform itself has not changed after a `updateTransform`. That would be done in a different PR.

## Another use-case of this PR

When the scene graph is being rendered, it is expected that `this._bounds` are update-to-date. However, calling `getLocalBounds()` previously changed what `getBounds(true)` returned. This is because `getLocalBounds()` would store its result in `this._bounds` and `getBounds(true)` wouldn't update `_bounds` (no transform update). This results in many errors throughout PixiJS (because the bounds returned by the node are incorrect).

This PR swaps `this._bounds` with another `this._localBounds`. This way `getLocalBounds` will not affect the result of `getBounds(true)`. Sadly though, it is still unable to prevent `getLocalBounds` from affecting the `getBounds(true)` value of grandchildren (and nodes below 1st generation children). I will work on a performant fix for that later on.

discussion_timeline.author: ShukantPal
discussion_timeline.body:
@bigtimebuddy We have a problem with parent containers whose local bounds depend on the transform of children in the parent’a reference frame.

I will push a fix for that, if possible.

@bigtimebuddy I have removed the sync barrier (stopping local-bounds recalculations) so there are no side-effects. I think @ivanpopelyshev would be okay to merge this now. (So this PR now only prevents getLocalBounds from storing its result in this._bounds, preventing corruption this.getBounds(true), via the _localBounds swap).

To prevent unnecessary bounds updates, we will need to implement a system where transform updates are propagated up the scene graph. This will be experimented on another branch.

issue_payload.body:
##### Description of change

As BitmapFont has now become much more accessible to our users thanks to recent efforts from the team, figured we could do with doing a bit of an optimisation pass for how bitmap fonts are rendering!

Main thing is that instead of rendering each letter as a sprite, we now render them as a mesh. This has a few benefits straight out of the box!

- lower memory footprint as we don't needs loads of sprites anymore, just a mesh or two
- faster creation `updateText`
    - pooling objects in this function.
    - including the meshes.
    - mesh buffers only reallocated if size grows.
- faster runtime `render`
    - as the text is either batched automatically if small. 
    - OR if its massive it is rendered in a single draw call (super fast, as no per character update is required)
    - tinting no longer required an `updateText` call as we leverage the mesh tint functionality.
- Ensure support for multipage fonts still works (made things a bit trickier :P)
- Added a couple of interfaces to some internal BitmapText bits.
- No surface API changes, all under the hood stuff.
- Character limit is about 11,000 - which is a lot of text :)


##### Pre-Merge Checklist

- [x] Documentation is changed or added
- [x] Lint process passed (`npm run lint`)
- [x] Tests passed (`npm run test`)

discussion_timeline.author: bigtimebuddy
discussion_timeline.body:
Wow great work! Thanks for doing this and putting in the effort. This has been high on my todo list. Directionally, removing Travis is the correct move.
 
The JSDoc bump is a consequential change. The new version of JSDoc misses a bunch of our documentation like events, and some deprecation. Version 3.6.x introduced a new parsing engine which screwed everything up. My preference would be to pin GitHub actions to node 10 until we can fix all those underlying issues as another PR. Because our typings also depend on JSDoc, this is a nontrivial change and requires a close attention.

Is that ismobilejs change a fix for #6511? Maybe we can do that as a separate PR?
